description: Directory names never traversed during discovery, the names deliberately traversed despite looking skippable, and the machine-local paths an operator excludes or admits. Names are portable across machines and ship non-empty; paths describe one machine's layout and ship empty. Replace or extend with CODESS_DISCOVERY_POLICY.

backup_conventions.note: Directory-name conventions for a kept-aside copy. A path segment matching one of these is excluded from Project candidacy: the tree below it is a copy of work that lives elsewhere, so admitting it would report one Project twice. Matching is case-sensitive and split by rule -- `OLD` matches a segment exactly, `Save` matches a segment that starts with it (`Save`, `Save2`, `Saved`). Case-sensitivity is deliberate: a directory named `old` in ordinary lowercase is a real name, not a backup marker.

traversed_on_purpose.conf: checked-in configuration, under a second spelling
traversed_on_purpose.credentials: pruning is not a security control; see security_note
traversed_on_purpose.data: fixtures, migrations, and seed files are versioned source
traversed_on_purpose.etc: checked-in configuration in many server projects
traversed_on_purpose.lib: a library's own source in C, Ruby, and Node layouts
traversed_on_purpose.private: access intent, not content kind: private source is still source
traversed_on_purpose.public: the served root of a web project, usually versioned
traversed_on_purpose.secrets: pruning is not a security control; see security_note
traversed_on_purpose.static: the served root, under a second spelling
traversed_on_purpose.web: the front-end half of a full-stack repository
traversed_on_purpose.windows: a platform port directory, not build output

security_note: Pruning stops traversal, which changes what is discovered rather than what is protected. A Session that already read a credential file records it whether or not Codess later walks that directory. Content exclusion is the content policy's subject. A name-based skip that looked like protection would be worse than none, because it invites trusting it.
editing_note: Add a name to a pruned group when your tree has a directory of that kind that is generated or transient. Move a name out of traversed_on_purpose only for your own tree: each is a source directory in a common layout, so pruning it hides the Project rather than the noise.
path_note: exclude_paths names trees on this machine that are not the operator's own work -- a collection kept for reference rather than developed in, which may hold one repository or fifty. include_paths admits a tree despite a rule that would skip it, which is why it outranks every other rule: name-based exclusion over-reaches by design. Both ship empty because a path is one machine's layout: a shipped default derived from one tree silently misclassifies directories on every other machine. CODESS_EXCLUDE_PATHS and CODESS_INCLUDE_PATHS supply them for one shell; this file is where a durable machine-level decision belongs.
precedence: include_paths > exclude_paths > exclude_dirs > hidden names > default traversal. Most specific wins, and an include_paths entry is honoured even where a parent is excluded and a segment name is on the pruned list.
syntax_note: Lists are comma-separated, not colon-separated: a colon is excluded from the value character set so a comma is unambiguous, and PATH notation would wrongly imply precedence by position. Whitespace is stripped. A name is alphanumeric with '-', '_', and '.' permitted, no '/', at most 255 characters; a path starts with '/', may end with one, and is at most 1023 characters. '..' is rejected in either, because a traversal segment lets an entry escape the scope it appears to name.
symlink_note: Symbolic links are not followed. Following them breaks the precedence rule: a link inside an excluded tree pointing into an included one re-admits excluded content by a path that never matches exclude_paths, so an exclusion the operator wrote is silently void. Links also admit cycles and report one Project twice under two paths. A tree that lives behind a link is admitted by naming its real location in include_paths.
name_note: exclude_dirs holds directory *names*, matched case-folded against every path segment. A name is portable -- `node_modules` under a JavaScript tree and `node_modules` under a Python one are both dependency stores -- so this list ships non-empty and is the same on every machine. exclude_paths and include_paths hold absolute paths, which describe one machine's layout, so both ship empty.
prefix_note: exclude_dir_prefixes matches a directory name by its leading characters, case-folded, and holds one entry: 'cmake-build-'. The mechanism was invented rather than borrowed, so it earns its place on one property no exact name has: CMake writes a directory per build configuration -- cmake-build-debug, cmake-build-release, cmake-build-relwithdebinfo, and any name a developer configures -- so the stem is the portable fact and the suffix is unbounded. Enumerating them is permanently incomplete, which is the same argument that made hidden names a rule rather than a list. Kept deliberately narrow: a prefix over-matches where an exact name cannot, so an entry belongs here only where a tool generates an open set of names from one stem, and 'build' or 'target' stay exact.
